# Introduction {.unnumbered}

`flexyBayes` specifies a mixed model once, in familiar ASReml-style or
`brms`-style formula syntax, and estimates it through any of three Bayesian
back ends: greta (TensorFlow Hamiltonian Monte Carlo), the integrated nested
Laplace approximation [@rue2009], or Stan via `brms` [@burkner2017]. A single
`fixed`/`random`/`rcov` specification is translated to back-end-specific code,
so the same model can be fitted three ways and the agreement between back ends
read as a robustness signal. The package targets agricultural mixed models and
is built to scale to large field-trial data.

A package that promises one specification across several estimation engines
makes two claims a reader is entitled to see checked. The first is
**correctness**: each back end must recover the right answer on a problem whose
answer is known independently. The second is **translation fidelity**: the model
the package builds for a back end must be the model the user wrote, so a
hand-written fit through the same engine must agree.

This study checks both, one back end at a time, against oracles the package did
not produce:

- A **fixed-effects exactness** check. For a Gaussian linear regression the
  posterior mean under a flat prior is the ordinary-least-squares solution, so
  the package result must match `stats::lm()` and the known data-generating
  coefficients to numerical precision.
- A **three-way Laplace-approximation** check on the `sleepstudy` data
  [@belenky2003]: `flexyBayes` through INLA against a hand-written
  `INLA::inla()` fit (translation fidelity) and against an `lme4` REML fit
  [@bates2015] (the independent reference).
- A **Hamiltonian-Monte-Carlo** check through greta [@golding2019] against the
  same `lme4` reference.
- A **Stan** check through `brms` against a standalone `brms::brm()` fit and the
  `lme4` reference.

Every figure below is computed by a benchmark script, cached, and read into the
text. No number is typed by hand. The benchmark scripts are reproduced verbatim
in the appendix, so a reader holding only this document can rerun each
comparison and confirm every value. Agreement on a random-effects model is
judged on the scale of the reference fit's standard error, the natural unit for
a parameter estimated with sampling noise. The fixed-effects check, which has an
exact answer, is judged on the absolute difference from `lm()`.
